title: I'll come the rest (Pesikta Rabbati 44)
hook: a far-off prince is told: come back as far as you can, and I'll come the rest
tomorrow: why are babies born with their fists closed?

segments.voice: Yesterday, an opening as small as a needle's eye, answered by one wide enough for wagons. A needle's eye. But some roads back feel longer than any opening.
screen: `A NEEDLE'S EYE.` → `SOME ROADS FEEL TOO LONG.`

segments.voice: A map app shows the whole route at once: hours of driving, dozens of turns, a little line that never seems to end. Sometimes the size of the trip is enough to keep you on the couch. The same happens with people, and with faith: the way back looks so long that the first step never happens. One question for today: what if the way back is too far?
screen: `THE WHOLE ROUTE AT ONCE.` → `TOO LONG TO START.` → `WHAT IF IT'S TOO FAR?`

segments.voice: Pesikta Rabbati answers with a parable, on the prophet's call: return, O Israel. A king's son was very far from his father. His friends told him: go back to your father. He said: I can't. It's too far. So his father sent word: come back as far as you're able, and I will come to you the rest of the way. That, says the midrash, is what God says in Malachi: "Return unto Me, and I will return unto you." Notice two things. The father doesn't pretend the distance is small. And he doesn't ask for the whole trip, only as far as you're able. Last week the voice at Sinai reached each person according to their strength. Here the road home works the same way. Now a neighbor. In Islam, a hadith qudsi, words the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, reports from God, recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari, says in effect: if My servant draws near to Me a hand's span, I draw near an arm's length; if he comes to Me walking, I come to him running. Shared ground: the human step is small, and God's answering step is bigger. The honest difference: the midrash is about a son who has wandered and must turn back, teshuvah, return. The hadith describes any servant drawing near, with no wandering assumed, and God more than matching each step. Each says it in its own words, from its own sources.
screen: `A SON TOO FAR AWAY.` · `AS FAR AS YOU'RE ABLE.` · `WALKING, AND GOD COMES RUNNING.` · `TURNING BACK, OR DRAWING NEAR.` · then, large: `I'LL COME THE REST.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and picture the road back to something you've drifted from: a person, a practice, a place. Take one step along it in your mind, only as far as you can honestly go today, and stop there. Then rest where you are, and leave the rest of the road open.
screen: `THE ROAD BACK.` · `ONE HONEST STEP.` · `LEAVE THE REST OPEN.`

segments.voice: I'll come the rest: the king's promise in Pesikta Rabbati. Come back as far as you're able, and I will come to you the rest of the way.
Your line: I'll come the rest. In the parable, nobody asked the son to walk the whole road.

howItsDone: Jews read Hosea 14, 'Return, O Israel', on Shabbat Shuvah, the Sabbath between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and this parable of the far-off prince is a familiar way of teaching teshuvah, return.

fork.setup: your friend stopped going to youth group a year ago. she says going back would mean explaining the whole year. by the parable, what's a fair first move?

teshuvah.meaning: Hebrew: return; turning back to God

notes: Malachi 3:7 quoted from JPS 1917 ('Return unto Me, and I will return unto you'); confirm.

Pesikta Rabbati 44 paraphrased; the text gives the distance as a journey of a hundred days, left out here under the claims rule ('very far'). Confirm the parable's wording and that the friends' advice and the son's 'I can't' are in the text.

Unity thread (wisdom day): the hadith qudsi in Sahih al-Bukhari (7405; also Sahih Muslim 2675), paraphrased in its own terms ('says in effect'), with 'peace be upon him' at the Prophet's first mention. Shared: the human step is small and God's answering step is bigger. Honest difference: the midrash is a son who has wandered turning back (teshuvah); the hadith describes any servant drawing near, with no wandering assumed. No ranking. Confirm the hadith number and that a Muslim and a Jewish reader would both find it fair.
Gloss 'Sahih al-Bukhari: a major collection': 'major' is descriptive, not a superlative; soften if needed. Glosses for Arabic terms carry no script (this path's gloss script is Hebrew only).
